analysis.one_liner: Bars law enforcement and intelligence agencies from buying Americans' location and phone records from data brokers without a warrant.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 21 bipartisan cosponsors but died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop government agencies from buying Americans' personal data — like phone location records and web browsing history — from third-party brokers instead of getting a court order. If agencies got such data improperly, it could not be used as evidence in court. It also closes related side doors, requiring agencies to use the normal warrant and court processes to get Americans' records.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday Americans whose location, call records, and browsing history are currently bought by agencies from data brokers without a warrant. The bill applies the same legal standards to purchased data that already apply when the government demands records directly from a phone or internet company.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits law enforcement and intelligence agencies from obtaining Americans' customer or subscriber records, or data illegitimately obtained, from a third party in exchange for anything of value [S2].
Makes records obtained in violation of the ban, and evidence derived from them, inadmissible in any trial, hearing, or other proceeding [S2].
Requires a court order, applying the most stringent legal standard, before a third party can be compelled to hand over such records [S3].
Bars intermediary providers that deliver or store communications from divulging communication contents or customer records to the government outside the normal warrant process [S3].

Makes the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act the exclusive legal route for acquiring Americans' communications records, location data, web browsing history, and search history for foreign intelligence purposes inside the United States [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers lose a lucrative line of business selling location and consumer records to government agencies. Law enforcement and intelligence agencies lose a cheap shortcut around the warrant process and would have to use courts, which takes more time and money.

drawbacks.text: The ban only covers records obtained 'in exchange for anything of value,' so data a third party hands over for free outside the bill's terms may fall outside the prohibition [S3].
Legitimate law enforcement access to commercially available data would now require going to court, which agencies argue adds time and cost to investigations.
The evidence-exclusion rule means evidence gathered in violation of the ban could not be used even in prosecutions of serious crimes, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: agencies give up a fast, cheap way to track Americans, and in exchange everyone's location and communications records are protected by the same court process the Fourth Amendment already requires. The free-data loophole means the bill is not airtight, but it would still shut down the bulk of the purchased-data practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 21 bipartisan cosponsors, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Wyden introduced the bill on April 21, 2021, joined by 20 original cosponsors including Republicans Rand Paul, Mike Lee, and Steve Daines alongside Democrats and independent Bernie Sanders [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
That referral was the bill's final action; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the agencies that buy Americans' location records from them kept the warrant-free workaround; the bill died in committee without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines from the start: 17 of 48 Senate Democrats, 3 of 50 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 2 independents cosponsored [S4].

industries.note: The bill directly targets the business of selling location, call, and consumer records to government agencies in exchange for payment. Their revenue from government customers depends on agencies avoiding the warrant process, which is exactly what the public gets from the bill.

Agencies would lose the ability to buy Americans' records cheaply from brokers and would have to obtain court orders instead. The bill also makes illegally obtained records unusable as evidence, removing the practical payoff of the workaround.

industries.industry: Telecom and internet infrastructure companies (intermediary providers)
industries.note: Companies that deliver or store communications for phone and internet providers would face new restrictions on divulging customer records to the government. The restriction shields their customers' privacy rather than serving the companies' commercial interest.
